claims.text: High-thermal-conductivity substrates will enhance the magnetocaloric effect of as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA nanostructures relative to low-thermal-conductivity substrates.
High-thermal-conductivity substrates will reduce magnetic hysteresis in these nanostructures during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
The as-deposited films or nanoribbons retain deposition-derived nanoscale disorder and grain structure.
Substrate thermal conductivity can be varied while deposition parameters, nanostructure geometry, and composition are held fixed.
Heat-transfer rates limit the cycle frequency under the proposed low-applied-field operating conditions.
Differences in interfacial thermal dissipation modify local temperature gradients within the HEA nanostructures.
Differences in interfacial thermal dissipation induce different interface stress states within the HEA nanostructures.
A high-thermal-conductivity substrate provides enhanced heat sinking during rapid cooling and heating cycles.
Enhanced heat sinking reduces local thermal gradients in the nanostructures.
Reduced local thermal gradients minimize interface-induced stress.
Lower interface-induced stress produces a sharper and more abrupt magnetic phase transition.
A sharper magnetic phase transition increases the magnetocaloric temperature change per cycle.
A sharper magnetic phase transition narrows the magnetic hysteresis loop.
Thermal-transport limitations and interface stresses are the dominant factors controlling magnetic phase-transition dynamics in the stated low-dimensional, rapid-cycling regime.
Prior evidence provides trends linking heat-transfer and stress-related effects to magnetic behavior.
A lack of statistically significant or consistent substrate-dependent differences in both magnetocaloric response and hysteresis would falsify the proposed substrate-governance hypothesis.
